about: STREONAESHALCH (Whitby), 793-1066: Hild's double house on the cliff above the Esk, its quiet end, and the Danes' Hvitabyr that grows under it. One port. Written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/streonaeshalch.md and the spine; a draft for the user to overwrite. (?) marks what is not checked; 'invented' marks what the sources do not give. Between 793 and 1066 no person is recorded at this place by name, so every living person here is invented. Woven with the region on 7 Oct 2026: ties run both ways, beats pointed at their cards (Data/encounters/northumbria_irish_sea_793.json); the count of Dorestad's errand for this region lies at the Scar.

ports.summary: A house of monks and nuns on a high headland above the mouth of the Esk, founded by King Oswiu and ruled first by Hild, with a king's grave in its church and lay families at hearths along the cliff edge. There is no quay, no toll and no market place: a ship takes the ground on the sand inside the river mouth and deals at the cellar door. A merchant comes for jet picked up under the cliffs, for the house's cloth, wool and hides, and to sell it wine, wax, glass and colours for its books.
ports.seasons: Jet is gathered after the winter gales have brought the cliff down, so the best of it is on offer between Easter and midsummer. Salmon run the brown river in summer and autumn; wool comes after the shearing. The house keeps Saint Hild's day eight days before the end of November, after sailing has stopped, so only a ship that winters on this coast sees it. The harbour dries at every ebb and the river comes down fast and peat-brown after rain on the moors.

history.text: King Oswiu founds the monastery in thanks for his victory over Penda, with Hild as its first abbess, for men and women both. The year is 'about 657'.
history.source: Bede, Ecclesiastical History III.24 (memory); en.wikipedia Whitby Abbey; English Heritage, Whitby Abbey history

history.text: King Oswiu hears Colman for the custom of Iona and Wilfrid for the custom of Rome on the keeping of Easter, here, with Cedd interpreting, and chooses for Peter, who holds the keys.
history.source: Bede, Ecclesiastical History III.25 (memory); en.wikipedia Synod of Whitby

history.text: King Oswiu dies on 15 February and is buried in the church of Saint Peter here. King Edwin's body lies here too; his head is at York.
history.source: en.wikipedia Oswiu; en.wikipedia Edwin of Northumbria; Victoria County History, York North Riding vol. 2 (1923), Whitby

history.text: Hild dies on 17 November, aged 66. In her last year she founded the daughter house at Hackness, where the nun Begu saw her soul carried up by angels that night.
Bishop Trumwine flees here from Abercorn after the Picts' victory, lives out his days in the house and is buried in Saint Peter's.
history.source: en.wikipedia Trumwine of Abercorn; Bede IV.26 (memory)

history.text: A Life of Pope Gregory is written here, 'by a monk or, possibly, a nun': the oldest telling of the Angles and the angels. The year is 'about 713'.
history.source: en.wikipedia Gregory the Great; B. Colgrave, The Earliest Life of Gregory the Great (1968), not opened (?)

history.text: Abbess Aelfflaed, Oswiu's daughter, dies. She is the last head of the house whose name is known.
history.source: en.wikipedia Aelfflaed of Whitby; dossier section 3

history.text: On 8 June heathen men plunder Lindisfarne, up this same coast. Nothing is recorded of Streonaeshalch in this year.
Heathen men raid the mouth of the Tyne; their leader is killed and a storm wrecks their ships.
King Raedwulf is killed fighting heathen raiders, the first on this coast for forty years.
About now the run of small Northumbrian coins lost on the headland stops. The year is a guess from the finds.

The great army holds York; Kings Osberht and Aella are killed there on 21 March. It is said, by writers three hundred years later, that Streonaeshalch was laid waste by Ingwar and Ubba in these years and lay empty for more than two hundred. No writer of the time says so; the ground shows only that the house ends in the ninth century.
history.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 867 (avalon.law.yale.edu/medieval/ang09.asp); Victoria County History, York North Riding vol. 2, Whitby; English Heritage

history.text: Healfdene shares out the land of the Northumbrians and his men plough it. The Norse names come after this: Hvitabyr, Whitby, and Prestebi, the priests' farm.
history.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 876; en.wikipedia Whitby; Victoria County History, York North Riding vol. 2 (Prestebi is an 11th-century form)

history.text: King Edmund is said, in one tradition, to have carried Hild's bones south to Glastonbury; another says Gloucester. The year is not given: between 939 and 946.
history.source: en.wikipedia Hilda of Whitby; William of Malmesbury, Gesta pontificum iii.116, not opened (?)

history.text: Siward, earl at York from 1033 and of all Northumbria from 1041, holds Whitby with its outlier Sneaton, fifteen carucates. Nothing says he ever came.
history.source: Victoria County History, York North Riding vol. 2 (Domesday); Design/content/realms/northumbria_york.json

history.text: In September Harald of Norway and Tostig burn Scarborough, down the coast, on their way to the Humber. Whitby is not named. By now the headland is empty and a substantial town lies down by the harbour; the manor is reckoned at 112 pounds.
history.source: Design/content/realms/northumbria_york.json; English Heritage, Whitby Abbey history; Victoria County History, York North Riding vol. 2

eras.text: The watching years. The house is whole: the church with the kings in it, the writing house, the looms, the guest fire, hearths along the cliff edge. But news of Lindisfarne came down the coast in June 793 and of the Tyne a year after, and the abbess asks every shipman what he saw to the north. The house wants wine, wax and colours, and pays in cloth, jet, hides and a little silver. From 799 a sea chest lies above the tide line.

Forty quiet years. King Eanred reigns long and no sails come. The talk of moving the books has gone stale; new hands are at the desk and the door. The small coins of York pass at the cellar, baser each year, and are worth nothing south of the Humber: a merchant takes his price in goods.

Thinning. A king is killed by heathen men in 844 and the old fear comes back. Fewer brothers and sisters sing the hours; some cells stand shut; the brass coins stop coming about the middle of these years. The cliff-edge families still gather jet and still want salt, iron and news.

Empty. The great army has York. Nobody can say in what season the last of the house went or where: it is said the Danes came, and nobody who says it was there. The roofs are off the small churches; sheep graze among the name stones. A few lay families hold on by the river and sell jet and fish to any ship that asks nothing.

Hvitabyr. Healfdene's men have the land and plough it; the place has a new name in their mouths, and the law is the settlers' custom, reckoned in marks and ores. Boats lie on the sand by the river, not under the church. Up among the ruins a priest or two farm a patch the Danes call Prestebi. York is a kings' town of Danes and Dubliners, and its craftsmen want every lump of jet the shore gives.

A harbour under an earl. The last king at York is gone; earls rule for the kings in the south. English and Danish are one speech with two sets of endings here. Jet goes to York to be cut into rings, pins and small crosses; fish, wool and hides go with it. The headland is pasture and a graveyard.

The earl's manor. Whitby with Sneaton is Earl Siward's, then Tostig's, then Morcar's: a rich holding with a reeve, a hall by the harbour and many boats. In September 1066 the smoke of Scarborough is seen to the south. Three years later King William wastes the north, and in 1086 the book says of Whitby: nearly all waste.

sites.name: The sand under the East Cliff
sites.see: A narrow gap between two cliffs with a brown river running out of it, and inside, on the left hand, a shelf of hard sand where a boat sits upright when the tide leaves her. In front, two small tarred boats and a drift of black weed; behind and far above, the roofs of the house against the sky. Gulls, the river talking over stones, a smell of peat water, weed and wet rope.
sites.source: The harbour dries; spring tides rise near 5.8 m; flat rock scars either side of the mouth cover at half tide (Research/water_levels/north_and_norway.md; modern figures carried back). Where boats lay is not recorded: under the East Cliff is the dossier's inference. No pier or quay is recorded before 1066.

sites.name: The Scar
sites.see: A wide floor of flat grey rock running out from the foot of the cliff, bare at low water and gone at half tide. In front, a fresh fall of shale and clay with women and children turning it over; in the stone underfoot, coiled shapes like sleeping snakes. Behind, the cliff, wet and leaning. The pick of a knife on stone, kittiwakes, and when someone tries a lump at a small fire, a smell of coal.
sites.source: Jet was gathered by beachcombing, not quarrying, and burns with a coal smell (en.wikipedia Jet (gemstone)); Bede I.1 on its virtues. The coiled stones are the ammonites of this shore; the tale that Hild turned snakes to stone is later, of unknown date, and nobody tells it here in 793 (dossier section 7).

sites.name: The cellar door
sites.see: A long low building of stone footings and timber at the top of the cliff path, with a half-door on the seaward side and a beam scale hung in it. In front, bolts of grey and brown cloth, sacks of wool, a basket of rough black stones, a tub of salted salmon; behind, casks in the dark. A brother with a tally stick, and the wind getting at everything.
sites.source: No market place, toll or mint is recorded (dossier section 2, section 8): selling at the house's store is the game's. Stone footings north of the later church (Peers's dig of the 1920s, English Heritage research page). Cloth by inference from the spindle whorls and loom weights (memory, not opened) (?).

sites.name: The guest house
sites.see: One room with a hearth in the middle of the floor and benches along both walls, a door to the south out of the wind. In front, a board scored in squares with pieces of bone and one of black jet; a harp in a bag on a peg. Behind, a shuttered window that looks straight down on the sea. Peat smoke, barley broth, and a bell from the church cutting the talk short.
sites.source: A jet gaming piece of the Anglian period was found on the headland (English Heritage research page). The harp passed round at a feast here: Bede IV.24, Caedmon (Design/content/lore/texts_more.json bede_caedmon). Abbess Aelfflaed was known for care of the sick (en.wikipedia). Guests kept apart under one brother: the common rule of such houses; this building is not identified (?).

sites.name: Saint Peter's, where the kings lie
sites.see: A stone church on the highest ground, not large, lime-washed, with a porch to the north. Inside, lamps over two long slabs side by side and a third apart, and the altar beyond with a cloth of the house's own weaving. Men's voices from one side and women's from the other, never quite together. Cold stone, lamp oil, and salt on the lips from the walk up.
sites.source: The church of Saint Peter with the graves of Edwin (his body), Oswiu, Eanflaed, Aelfflaed and Bishop Trumwine (Bede III.24, IV.26, memory; en.wikipedia Oswiu, Edwin, Trumwine). The church has not been found and may lie under the later abbey church (?). A double house: whether it still was in 793 is not known.

sites.name: The writing house
sites.see: A narrow room with its windows to the north for the steady light, three sloped desks, and a chest with an iron hasp against the dry wall. In front, a nun ruling lines with a bone point, a horn of ink, a pot of red; on a shelf, styli of bronze and wax tablets. Behind, a boy scraping a skin stretched on a frame. The scratch of pens and somebody's cough.
sites.source: Writing styli and book mounts from the 1920s dig (memory, not opened) (?); the Life of Gregory written here about 713 by a monk or a nun (en.wikipedia Gregory the Great). The room is the game's.

sites.name: The hearths on the cliff edge
sites.see: A straggle of timber houses along the lip of the headland, each with its smoke, its pit and its heap of shells; between two of them a well with a hide bucket. In front, a woman at an upright loom in a doorway, the clay weights knocking; a man mending a net. Behind, nothing: the grass stops and the sea begins far below. Dogs, children, wood smoke and fish.
sites.source: Timber buildings, hearths, pits and wells of the Anglian period at the cliff edge; some 500 metres of the headland have since gone into the sea (English Heritage research page). Spindle whorls and loom weights (memory) (?).

sites.name: The byre and the home pasture
sites.see: A long turf-walled byre on the landward side of the house, its door facing away from the wind, and beyond it a walled pasture going back toward the moor. In front, small black cattle steaming in the morning and an old man leaning on the wall. Behind, heather to the edge of sight. Dung, hay, and the house bell coming thin across the field.
sites.source: Caedmon left the feast for the cattle shed, whose care was his that night, and was told in a dream to sing (Bede IV.24, memory; en.wikipedia Caedmon). The house's cowherd and reeve are in the same story. Calves are also the house's book skins.

sites.name: The graveyard south of the church
sites.see: Rows on rows of low graves on the south side, more than a visitor can count at a walk, with plain stone crosses the height of a child and small slabs cut with a name. In front, a stone with a cross and one word; behind, the church wall, and after 867 no roof on it. Wind in the grass. Later, sheep.
sites.source: Part of a large Anglian cemetery found in 2000 south of the church (English Heritage research page); the count of graves is not checked (?). The Corpus of Anglo-Saxon Stone Sculpture lists 56 pieces from the abbey, plain crosses and name stones among them (memory for the kinds). unlocks_793.json: a stone 'becun' can be had here before 900.

sites.name: Prestebi: the roofless cells
sites.see: The headland as the Danes found it: a scatter of small stone churches and cells without roofs, nettles in the doorways, the walls still shoulder high. In front, one cell thatched again with a smoke hole and a patch of beans beside it; behind, the old church open to the sky. Larks, wind, and from the one roofed cell a man's voice singing an office alone.
sites.source: About 1078 Reinfrid found some forty roofless 'monasteria vel oratoria' here (Victoria County History, Yorkshire vol. 3, Whitby Abbey). Prestebi, 'the priests' farm', is an 11th-century name and suggests priests living here in Danish times (Victoria County History, York North Riding vol. 2). The one thatched cell is the game's (?).

sites.name: Hvitabyr: the booths by the river
sites.see: Low houses and boat sheds on the flat ground inside the river mouth, on both banks, with boats drawn up between them bow to the land. In front, fish on racks, a trestle of jet lumps and half-cut rings, a set of folding scales; behind, the cliff and the empty headland. From 1033 a long hall with carved door posts stands above the booths. Two tongues at once, hammering, tar and drying fish.
sites.source: By 1066 'there was a substantial town called Whitby down by the harbour' (English Heritage). Hvitabyr is the settlers' name (en.wikipedia Whitby). Northmen made rings and small beasts of jet; York's jet workers flourish in the 10th century (en.wikipedia Jet; goods_793.json jet). Earl Siward's manor before 1066 (Victoria County History). The hall and the booths are the game's: nothing has been dug.

sites.name: The salmon reach
sites.see: The river a little way above the landing, brown as ale, sliding between alder banks with the tide pushing up under it. In front, a wattle fence run out from the bank and a man standing in the water to his thighs with a long net; behind, oak woods climbing toward the moor. Water over stones, a heron, and the clean cold smell of the river.
sites.source: Salmon and sea trout run the Esk, a moorland river quick to flood, tidal about 3 km up to Ruswarp (en.wikipedia River Esk, North Yorkshire; modern facts carried back). The fish fence is the game's (?).

people.name: Eadswith
people.trait: A king's distant kinswoman who rules monks and nuns alike without raising her voice; practical, a good hand with a wound, and slow to be frightened.
people.want: To know what is truly coming down the coast, and to decide once, and rightly, whether the books and the bones stay on the cliff.
people.fear: That she will be the abbess under whom King Edwin's grave was opened by strangers.
people.voice: Asks plain questions and waits for the whole answer. Thanks people by name. Does not say 'perhaps'.
people.looks: About fifty, tall, spare, a weathered face; a dark wool gown and a white linen veil pinned with two plain bronze pins; a ring of keys at her girdle and a small knife for lancing.
knows: who lies in the church and who put them there
what the house needs this year and what it can pay
how to clean and close a wound, and which crewman should not sail yet
what the archbishop at York will allow and what he need not be asked

ties.note: brought her into the house as a child and gave her the desk
her eyes at the door and the beach; she trusts his count
the two houses pray for each other's dead; she wants his counsel on moving the saints
the house is in his diocese; she asks his leave late and sparingly
feeds him whenever he walks in, and counts the books when he walks out
the old cowherd has outlived two abbesses and means to try for a third; she lets him

lines.greet: You came from the north or the south? If the north, sit. Tell me what you saw with your own eyes, and leave out what you heard.
lines.greet_again: The merchant. Good. Hunwine says your count was right last time. Is the island's bishop still on his island?
rumour: They saw the sails from Bebbanburg's rock and did not come down. I ask myself who would come down for us.
Hackness is a day's walk from salt water. Our sisters there sleep sound. I have begun to think that is worth something.
A king is under that slab without his head. York kept the head. Nobody asked the king.
lines.saying: Mother Hild's rule was simple: nobody here is rich and nobody here goes without. It is harder than it sounds.
lines.farewell: Go with God and watch the sea for us. If you see a long hull where no trade is, come and tell me before you tell anyone.

people.source: invented. No abbess is named after Aelfflaed's death in 714 (dossier sections 3 and 8). Aelfflaed's surgery: en.wikipedia. Hild's rule 'that no one there was rich and none poor': Bede IV.23 (memory). Edwin's body here and head at York: Victoria County History. Name: Ead- + -swith.

people.name: Sigethryth
people.trait: The nun who keeps the writing house: quick, curious, pleased with her own hand, and unable to leave a riddle alone.
people.want: Calfskin, red lead and the yellow that looks like gold; and for something she has written to be read somewhere she will never go.
people.fear: Fire, damp, and that everything this house knows is in one chest.
people.voice: Talks fast, stops to think with the pen in her mouth, then finishes the sentence exactly. Laughs at her own jokes first.
people.looks: Late twenties, small, bright-eyed, ink on the side of her right hand; a dark gown with the sleeves tied back, a linen veil, a bronze stylus on a cord and a penknife at her belt.
knows: what books the house holds, and that the Life of Pope Gregory was written at this very desk
the house hands of Lindisfarena, Gyrwe and York at a glance
English verse by heart, Caedmon's song among it, and a good many riddles
what a book costs in calves, days and colours

ties.note: they lend each other exemplars and insults by the same ship
borrows from Torhtred at Bede's house and sends him red lead when she has it
her abbess, who taught her her letters
he borrows books for York and brings them back late, or lighter
knows his hand from Gyrwe's school leaves and asks after his brother
never met him; has his riddles for Pippin by heart from a copy Sigewine left
he brings her the calf skins and takes a verse in payment
the cliff boy who carries her letters down to the boats and her skins up, and is paid in red lead for his mother's wool

lines.greet: Wipe your hands before you come past the door. Thank you. Now: do you carry skins, or colours, or only questions?
lines.greet_again: You again, and the tide with you. Did Ceolhelm send an answer, or only his opinion of my letter forms?
rumour: A book this house made says the English boys in Rome's market were not Angles but angels. We said it first. Write that down somewhere.
Sigewine borrowed our Orosius at Candlemas. It is past harvest. Monks of York keep Lent better than they keep promises.
One chest, one hasp, one roof of thatch. I think about that every time someone carries a candle past me.
lines.saying: The pen is three fingers' work and the whole body's ache. Still, it is the only plough that sows for a thousand years.
lines.farewell: Keep whatever I gave you flat and dry, and ask at every writing house what they lack. God speed your keel.

people.source: invented. The Life of Gregory written here about 713 'by a monk or, possibly, a nun' is the oldest telling of the Angles and angels (en.wikipedia Gregory the Great; memory). lindisfarena.json has Ceolhelm writing to this house for exemplars. The three-fingers complaint is the common scribes' colophon, in our own words. Name: Sige- + -thryth.

people.name: Hunwine
people.trait: The brother who keeps the guest fire and the cellar door: sociable, exact about weights, and far too fond of the board game for a monk.
people.want: Wine and wax for the altar bought at a fair price; a guest who can give him a hard game.
people.fear: Short measure found in his cellar, and the abbess finding the jet king in his sleeve during the night office.
people.voice: Easy and cheerful, with a number in every second sentence. Says the price once and then talks about something else.
people.looks: Mid forties, round-shouldered, a monk's cropped crown going grey, a brown habit hitched for the cliff path; a tally stick in his belt and a black gaming piece he turns in his fingers.
knows: the price of everything the house buys and sells, and what the last three ships asked
which coins pass here and that York's do not pass south of the Humber
who has slept at the guest fire this year and where they were going
every opening on the board, and who on this coast plays it well

ties.note: answers to her for every cask
pays him in ale to say which ship is worth walking down for
the two cellarers have argued the price of wax by letter for ten years
sends Dunwald salt fish up the coast when the Tyne is poor, and gets lamp oil back
the only man who beats him at the board, and never says so
likes a Frisian who gives the worst news first

lines.greet: Thanks be to God, a sail. Come up to the fire. Broth first, prices after, and the board after that if you play.
lines.greet_again: I kept your place on the bench and your last move in my head. You were losing. Sit down.
rumour: Wax is dear this year. I am told the bees of Francia have turned heathen and keep it for themselves.
The king's coin will buy you a loaf here and a laugh at Lundenwic. Take cloth. Cloth is the same in every tongue.
A Frisian slept here at Whitsun bound for the Tyne. He asked twice how far York was by water, and did not go.
lines.saying: Weigh it in front of the man and you need never weigh his friendship after.
lines.farewell: The path is slippery after rain; hold the rope. Come back before Martinmas and I will have wool for you.

people.source: invented. The jet gaming piece is real (English Heritage research page). Northumbrian coin does not travel south of the Humber (Design/content/realms/northumbria_york.json). The porter's 'Thanks be to God' is the Rule of St Benedict ch. 66 (wording to check (?)). Name: Hun- + -wine.

people.name: Cudda
people.trait: The boatman under the cliff: unhurried, knows the scars and the river bar by the colour of the water, and walks the tide line every morning before anyone else.
people.want: First sight of whatever the sea leaves; a new boat before the old one drowns him.
people.fear: A north-easter on the ebb, and a long hull seen too late.
people.voice: Slow and flat, eyes on the water while he talks. Answers a question with what the tide is doing.
people.looks: Near forty, short, bow-legged, a face like tanned hide and a grey-streaked beard; a patched wool tunic, bare feet, a sounding pole and a lump of jet on a thong at his neck.
knows: when the scars cover and when there is water over the river bar
how the Esk comes down after rain on the moor, and where a boat is safe from it
what ships passed this week, and which way
where on the shore the cliff has fallen, and so where the jet is

ties.note: tells him which ship is in before she touches
his wife's brother, the pilot under the kings' rock
they have sheltered in each other's water and owe each other a boat hook
meets the Tyne boats on the herring in autumn; they share a short name less one letter and a long thirst
taught the boy the tide line; from 799 the chest was their secret for one morning
two men who count tides; they talk for an hour in twenty words

lines.greet: You came in on the last of the flood. Sensible. She will sit on the sand by noon. Mind the rock on your steer-board hand going out.
lines.greet_again: I knew the sail. The river is up after the rain, so lie higher than you did. I will show you.
rumour: The cliff came down past the second scar at Candlemas. There will be black stone in it. I have not told the cellar yet.
The sea gives. It gave me a cask once, and once a man. The cask was the better company.
I watch north in the mornings now. I never used to look north. Nothing came from the north but weather.
lines.saying: The tide waits for the abbess and the king the same: not at all.
lines.farewell: Go on the top of the water and keep off till you see the roofs small. Then turn as you please.

people.source: invented. Scars, range and the drying harbour: Research/water_levels/north_and_norway.md. The sea chest of 799: riddles_793.json riddle_exeter_03_storm_sky and the spine. Name: Cudda, an English short name of the attested kind (?). He fishes, pilots and combs the tide line.

people.name: Hwaetred
people.trait: The house's old cowherd, a layman: sly, patient, tone-deaf, and the keeper of the byre where another cowherd once learned to sing.
people.want: A warm corner, a game of the board, and someone new to tell about Caedmon.
people.fear: The harp coming round to him. He has dodged it for fifty years.
people.voice: Dry and slow, with a long wait before the last word. Speaks of cattle as people and people as cattle.
people.looks: Past sixty, lean and bent, white stubble, a hooded cloak of undyed wool the colour of his cows; a hazel stick polished by his hand and a wooden cup on his belt.
knows: Caedmon's song, every word, though he will only say it, not sing it
what the house's calves, hides, cheese and wool are worth before the cellarer adds his share
the moor tracks inland to Hackness and how long a cart takes
weather by the cattle: which way they lie before wind

ties.note: beats him at the board and lets him think otherwise
brings her the calf skins; she writes his sayings in margins
has herded for three abbesses and outlived two
a Northman who knows riddles is worth an evening; neither asks the other's god

lines.greet: A shipman. Then you will be wanting hides, and I will be wanting news. Lean on the wall. The wall does not mind.
lines.greet_again: The red cow calved since you were here. That is my news. Yours had better be longer.
rumour: It was this byre. He lay down there by the door, and a man in a dream said: sing me the beginning of things.
I have slept in that same straw fifty years. Nobody came. I think heaven had heard my voice already.
Every calf I rear, the nun wants its skin. I tell them at birth: you will be a psalm, be proud.
lines.saying: When the harp comes round, a wise man remembers his cattle.
lines.farewell: The cows are lying with their backs to the sea. Wind by evening. Go now or stay for supper.

people.source: invented. Caedmon, the cowherd of this house, about 670-680: Bede IV.24 (Design/content/lore/texts_more.json bede_caedmon; story/town_games_793.json). Name: Hwaet- + -red.

people.name: Heremod
people.trait: A cliff man of the lay hearths: climbs for eggs and birds in spring, gathers jet after every fall, and in old age is the last person here who remembers the house full.
people.want: A fair price for the black stone, paid in things and not in the king's bad brass; later, only to be told where the sisters went.
people.fear: The rope, the cliff, and dying as the only one who knows the names on the stones.
people.voice: Short sentences, a cliff man's habit of saying only what is sure. When old, he begins everything with 'when the bell still rang'.
people.looks: As a young man: wiry, wind-burned, fair hair tied back, a rope of twisted hide over one shoulder, a bag of black stones and a short iron pick. When old: the same rope, white hair, one stiff knee.
knows: true jet from the soft black shale that looks like it: by rubbing, by weight and by fire
where the cliff is about to come down
who on the headland is leaving and who has gone, in the thinning years
after 867: what the place was, and which stone is whose

ties.note: learned the tide line from him as a boy
carries her letters down to the boats and her skins up
the old man's grandsons gather jet on a shore the Dane now calls his
sent word north, when the house thinned, asking where its people should go (?)

lines.greet: Jet? Hold out your hand. Feel the weight: light as wood. Now rub it on your sleeve and pick up that straw with it.
lines.greet_again: I kept the big piece back for you. The cellar offered brass. You pay in iron and salt, so you get the big piece.
rumour: The king's coins get yellower every year. Soon we will be paid in kettle. I would sooner have the kettle.
When the bell still rang there were forty roofs up there. I thatched some. Count them now.
Nobody burned us, whatever they say at York. One spring there were fewer. Then a door was left open all winter.
lines.saying: Jet is known by the fire and a neighbour by the hard winter.
lines.farewell: Keep it wrapped; it chips. And if a man offers you black stone that is heavy, he is selling you the cliff.

people.source: invented. Jet 'being warmed with rubbing holds fast whatever is applied to it, like amber', and smells of coal on the fire: Bede I.1; en.wikipedia Jet. The base stycas of the 9th century: Design/content/realms/northumbria_york.json. The house 'abandoned at some point in the 9th century; we do not know exactly when or how': English Heritage. His line about nobody burning it is one reading, not a fact. Name: Here- + -mod.

people.name: Ketil
people.trait: One of Healfdene's men who got land at the river mouth in the sharing: a careful farmer and part-time trader with an English wife, more interested in ploughs than in swords now.
people.want: His land held without dispute, a steady buyer for jet and fish, and peace in his own house, where his wife wants a priest for the children.
people.fear: A new king at York who shares the land again; and, though he would not say it, the dead under the stones on the headland.
people.voice: Says less than he means, in an English with Danish bones. Understatement for anything large.
people.looks: Thirties when first met, thick-set, red-brown beard plaited once, a blue wool tunic to the knee, a silver arm ring he cuts pieces from to pay, a small iron hammer on a thong under his shirt.
knows: the settlers' law here: marks and ores, and whose word stands surety for whose
what York's kings and craftsmen pay for jet
which ships on this coast trade and which take
that a priest lives among the ruins, and that his own wife feeds him

ties.note: the old cliff man's kin gather on Ketil's shore and both know it was theirs first
if Ravn's name is said, he remembers it: a riddle-man of the old king's hall, spoken of in his father's house
Grim, the earl's reeve five generations on, counts him as the first of his line here
the daughter of his old shipmate in the army, who keeps an ale-house at York: he sends her jet and gulls' eggs, and she sends him the kings' names

lines.greet: You may lie on the sand. Nobody will touch her. I say so, and it is my sand, more or less.
lines.greet_again: The merchant. You look well. My wife said you would drown; she is seldom wrong, so I am a little surprised.
rumour: We shared the land by the rope. I got the river mouth and the wind. Others got the good earth and the neighbours.
There is a priest up among the stones. He does no harm. He prays for my barley, my wife says; it came up, so let him.
The men at York pay silver for black stone and make rings of it. I do not ask why a man wants a black ring.
lines.saying: The farm is small, but it is under my own feet.
lines.farewell: Go carefully. The sea here is not bad, for a sea.

people.source: invented. 876: 'Healfden divided the land of the Northumbrians; so that they became afterwards their harrowers and plowers' (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle). Law in marks and ores south of the Tees from 876 (Design/content/realms/northumbria_york.json). Prestebi: Victoria County History. His saying turns Havamal 36 ('better a house, though a hut it be', Bellows 1923) into our own words. Name: Ketil, a common Norse name.

people.name: Grim
people.trait: Reeve of the earl's manor of Whitby and Sneaton: a harbour man with a Danish name and an English tongue, fair, busy, and proud of how much the place renders.
people.want: The manor's dues in on time, ships that come back, and no earl ever riding out to look for himself.
people.fear: Ships from Norway; and, after the autumn of 1066, soldiers from the south.
people.voice: Brisk, counting on his fingers, with settlers' words for everything to do with boats and land.
people.looks: About forty, broad, clipped fair beard, a good red cloak with a silver ring-pin, a small jet cross at his throat; a notched tally and a bunch of keys.
knows: what the manor owes the earl and what a ship owes the manor
who is earl this year, and what that changes: Siward, then Tostig, then Morcar
the price of jet at York and who cuts it best
the old stories of the headland, at fifth hand and all different

ties.note: counts Ketil as the first of his line here
sends fish north to Saint Cuthbert's people in Lent, and gets prayers and gossip back
his father held his land by King Cnut's peace, and Grim keeps the king's writ in the manor chest
the wright at York, to whom he sends any wrecked timber worth saving, and from whom he gets a mended boat a year
the widow at York who buys his raw jet for the cutters on her plot, and pays on the day
the earl's reeve on the rock in the north: they send each other word of where the York tax man is this week

lines.greet: Welcome to Whitby. Lie where the boy shows you. The earl's due is taken on what you sell, not on what you carry past.
lines.greet_again: Back, and before the herring. Good. I have jet put by and a York man asking for it; outbid him if you like.
rumour: They say a holy woman turned snakes to stone up there. My grandmother said it was the Danes did the turning. Somebody is wrong.
Earl Siward has never set foot here. That is the best thing I know about him, God keep him.
Smoke to the south yesterday, a great deal of it. Scarborough way. I have had the boats pulled up above the sheds.
lines.saying: A harbour is a field that ploughs itself, twice a day.
lines.farewell: Fair wind. If you meet ships from the north with shields on the rail, I would thank you to come back and say so.

people.source: invented. Earl Siward held Whitby and Sneaton, 15 carucates, a manor reckoned at 112 pounds before 1066 (Victoria County History, York North Riding vol. 2); nothing says he ever came (dossier section 3). Scarborough burnt in September 1066 (realms/northumbria_york.json). The snakestone tale is of unknown date (dossier section 7): he is given it as hearsay only, in the 11th century (?). An earl's due on sales is the game's: no toll is recorded. Name: Grim, common in Yorkshire's Domesday.

stories.title: Whether the saints should go inland
stories.summary: After June 793 the abbess watches the sea and asks whether the books and the bones of the kings should be moved out of reach of ships. She will not decide on rumour: she wants to know what the bishop on the plundered island would do, and what York will allow. The merchant carries the question, and then, if she chooses, the chest.
stories.picture: An abbess in a white veil standing at the edge of a high cliff at evening, one hand shading her eyes, looking north over an empty grey sea; behind her a small lime-washed church with a lamp in its door.

beats.text: Eadswith asks what was seen at Lindisfarena, and whether its bishop has moved Saint Cuthbert. She asks the merchant to put her question to Higbald himself, since he is going that way or knows who is. (Sets st_question_carried.)

Higbald hears the question out. His answer is short: the saint chose his island and stays; but books can be written twice and bones cannot, so let her copy what she has and send the copies where no ship comes. (Sets st_higbald_answered.)

The archbishop's clerk says the minster would gladly keep the house's books 'for copying', and is vaguer about giving them back. The bones of a king are another matter and need the archbishop's own word.

The answer is read to the abbess and the scribe. Three ways lie open: leave all as it is and keep a watch; cart the book chest to the sisters at Hackness; or have Sigethryth copy the house's own Life of Pope Gregory and let the merchant carry the copy over the sea.
The copy is handed to Sigewine, or to a priest bound up the Rhine, for a house in the south that lacks it. He reads the first leaf standing on the dam and forgets to say thank you.
The headland is roofless. Whatever was sent away is what is left of the house; whatever stayed is under the nettles. The merchant, or his heir, can stand in the open church and know which it was.

endings.how: You brought back Higbald's answer and the abbess chose to move nothing, or you never carried the question.
endings.text: The books and the kings stay where Hild put them. For two generations it looks like the right choice. After 867 nobody can say where any of it went.
endings.reward: Eadswith's thanks and the guest bench (streonaeshalch.guest_bench); the deed carried_letters. Nothing of the house's outlasts it.

endings.how: You paid for the iron-bound chest and the cart (the work streonaeshalch.work.hackness_chest) and saw the books go inland.
endings.text: The best of the books go a day's walk from salt water, to the sisters at Hackness. The writing house keeps working copies. When the cliff falls silent, Hackness still has a lamp for a while.
endings.reward: Flag bk_carried; Sigethryth a fast friend (copy_text at no cost here); the house's commission prices better by a tenth until 867. The heir is known at Hackness.

endings.how: You paid for skins and had the Life of Gregory copied, and carried the copy to Dorestad for a house in the south.
endings.text: One copy of a book made on this cliff goes up the Rhine in a stranger's bag. A thousand years on, the only copy of it left in the world lies in a monastery by the mountains, far from any sea.
endings.reward: Flags bk_carried and bk_knows_worth; the scribe's friendship; a letter of thanks that opens the writing house at Traiectum; the deed carried_letters with churchmen everywhere.

stories.reward: The abbess and the scribe as friends for life, the book road's flags, and the knowledge, for the heir, of what the house's choice came to.

stories.title: What the sea gave Cudda
stories.summary: After the wrecking storms of 799 a sea chest lies above the tide line under the East Cliff. In it, dry in a waxed cloth, is a leaf of English verse: the third of three scattered from Lindisfarena's writing house, the storm in the sky. Sigethryth knows the hand at a glance and knows whose it is.
stories.picture: A small iron-bound chest half sunk in wet sand and black weed at the foot of a great cliff at dawn, a bow-legged boatman crouched over it with a sounding pole across his knees, lifting out a folded cloth.

beats.text: Ceolhelm sells a copy of the first leaf, the storm on the land, and says two more went astray.
A brother at Bede's house has the second leaf, the storm under the sea.

Cudda, or after 822 the cliff man Heremod, shows what the sea left: a chest with a foreign lock, a knife, a comb, and a leaf of verse in a waxed cloth. He cannot read it and wants to know if it is worth ale or silver. (Gives the text exeter_03_storm_sky and the riddle riddle_exeter_03_storm_sky.)

Sigethryth reads it aloud, once in English and once slowly for a Frisian ear. 'That is Lindisfarena's hand, and Ceolhelm's ruling: he always crowds the last line.' She will not say the answer. She says the leaf itself says who is asked.
With all three answers, the pilot under the kings' rock can be asked about the gut among the Farne islands.

endings.how: You paid Cudda for the leaf, solved it and kept it in the chest.
endings.text: The third leaf is the house's. With the other two it names a landing no other ship uses.
endings.reward: give_text exeter_03_storm_sky; the riddle's own reward (rw_standing_small); with all three, the cove among the Farnes (rw_cove_farne, bebbanburg.farne_cove). Cudda friendly.

endings.how: You let Sigethryth copy the leaf and carried the leaf itself back to Ceolhelm at Lindisfarena.
endings.text: Ceolhelm turns it over twice, says the sea has not improved the margins, and puts it back in its quire with his own hands.
endings.reward: You keep a fair copy (the text and the riddle all the same); both scribes fast friends; free copying at both writing houses; the deed carried_letters.

endings.how: You told Cudda it was worth nothing and bought it for a cup of ale.
endings.text: Cudda finds out its worth from the nun within the month. He still pilots you in, and takes his time about it.
endings.reward: The leaf for almost nothing; Cudda cool, and his pilotage dearer by half until you make it right with a gift.

stories.reward: The third storm leaf, and with its fellows a harbour of the house's own; either way a scribe here who knows the merchant by name.

stories.title: When the harp comes round
stories.summary: On a feast night the guest house keeps the old custom: the harp goes from hand to hand and each one sings. It comes toward the merchant. A hundred years ago a cowherd of this house got up at that moment and went out to the cattle, and what happened in the byre is why the house still tells it.
stories.picture: A firelit room of benches at night, a small harp being passed along a row of laughing faces toward a merchant who is half risen from his seat; in the open door behind him, the dark and one cow's pale face.

beats.text: After supper the harp starts down the bench. Hunwine sings badly and is cheered. Two places away, the old cowherd Hwaetred stands up, says something about a cow, and leaves. The harp comes on.

Hwaetred is sitting in the straw by the door. He says this is the place, and says Caedmon's song through, flat as a tally: now we must honour heaven's guardian. He will say it as often as it takes to learn.
Sigethryth will write the nine lines out fair, in English as it was sung and with the Latin beside it as Bede gave it, for the price of the skin.
At the minster's guest table the song is known and loved. A merchant who can say it right, in Northumbrian, is not quite a stranger any more.

endings.how: You took the harp and sang what you had: a Frisian rowing song, or whatever your tongue holds.
endings.text: It is not good and nobody minds. The bench makes room. Hunwine asks for the words afterwards and gets them wrong for years.
endings.reward: The crew's heart up; Hunwine and the guest house friendly at once; a song to trade at any English guest fire (act:song pays a little better).

endings.how: You remembered your boat as the cowherd remembered his cattle, went out, and found Hwaetred.
endings.text: You learn Caedmon's song from the one man here who will not sing it. Nobody dreams anything. The cows are warm.
endings.reward: Caedmon's song by heart (a text for the chest, if the integrator adds one); Hwaetred a friend, and with him the house's hides and calves at the byre's price.

endings.how: You, or Ravn at your elbow, passed the harp on and set the bench a riddle.
endings.text: The monks take it as a fair exchange and argue the answer until the bell. Sigethryth hears of it by morning and wants it written down.
endings.reward: The deed won_riddle here if they do not guess; the scribe curious about you; a riddle offered back from the house's own store.

stories.reward: A place on the bench by name, and the oldest English song there is, learned where it was made.

stories.title: Black and bright
stories.summary: Jet is the one thing this shore has that nowhere else does, and most of what is sold as jet elsewhere is black shale. The cliff people teach the merchant Bede's tests, and the stone finds its buyers: churchmen first, then the ring-cutters of Danish York and the Northmen's towns beyond.
stories.picture: A weathered hand holding a rough black stone over a small fire on a rock shelf, another lump being rubbed on a wool sleeve with bits of straw clinging to it; grey sea and a fallen cliff behind.

beats.text: A cliff man shows the three tests. True jet is light in the hand; rubbed warm it lifts a straw, as amber does; and a crumb on the fire burns and smells of coal. He adds, as his grandmother did, that the smoke drives off snakes. (Sets st_knows_jet.)
A dealer offers 'northern jet', heavy and dull. It will not lift a straw. A merchant who knows can say so before witnesses, or buy it cheap and sell it on.
In the craftsmen's street they cut jet into finger rings, pins, dice and small crosses, and pay for raw lumps by weight, in silver, with no questions.
The foreigners' town on the Liffey buys jet for arm rings and gaming pieces. Tested stone from the cliff itself fetches half as much again as it does at York.
Ketil, or his heirs, will keep the season's best pick for one buyer who comes every year before midsummer and pays in what the settlement lacks.
The count's steward at Dorestad tries the stone with a straw at the hall door. His lord's chaplain had read of it in the English priest's book, and the count wants a cross of it for his chapel.

endings.how: You bought fairly at the Scar for three seasons running and sold only tested stone.
endings.text: The cliff families keep the big pieces back for your sail. Buyers at York and Dublin learn that jet from your hull needs no trying.
endings.reward: The unlock streonaeshalch.first_pick (buy_at_source for jet before the cellar or the booths see it); the deed fair_dealing at Eoforwic and Duiblinn.

endings.how: You bought heavy black shale cheap and sold it as jet where nobody knew the tests.
endings.text: It pays once, well. Then a ring cracks on a York man's finger and he remembers the ship.
endings.reward: A quick profit of perhaps 60 d a sack; then standing lost at the port where it was sold, and Heremod will not show you the falls again.

endings.how: At Lundenwic you showed the straw test before witnesses and named the false stone.
endings.text: The dealer is laughed out of the row. The reeve's man remembers who knew the difference.
endings.reward: The deed fair_dealing at Lundenwic; a standing order for true jet from a goldsmith there, at a third over the common price.

stories.reward: A trade nobody else on the chart can do as well: jet at the cliff's price, and the knowledge to prove it true.

stories.title: The priests' farm
stories.summary: When the land is shared out in 876 a Dane called Ketil gets the river mouth, and with it a ruined headland where one priest still sings in a thatched cell. Ketil's English wife wants her children christened; Ketil wants no trouble with his own people. A merchant who is known to both sides can stand between them.
stories.picture: A red-bearded farmer with a hammer amulet and a thin tonsured priest facing each other across a field wall, roofless stone cells behind the priest and a river mouth with drawn-up boats behind the farmer; between them a woman holding a child.

beats.text: The house is gone. An old cliff man, Heremod, or his kin, says what he saw: no burning, only fewer each spring, and then a door left open. He says it is told otherwise at York.

Ketil has the land and a new name for it. He mentions, as a thing of no importance, that his wife feeds a priest up among the stones, and that some of his neighbours think the stones would build a good hall.

York has a Christian Dane for king, Guthred, and an archbishop again. A clerk of the minster will send chrism and a hand bell to Prestebi if someone trusted by the settlers carries them and stands surety for the priest. (Sets en_hostage_given when the surety is sworn.)
The bell is hung, or it is not. Ketil comes up the path on the day, stands outside the wall with his arms folded, and stays to the end.

endings.how: You carried the bell and the chrism from York and swore surety for the priest before Ketil and his neighbours.
endings.text: Ketil's children are christened in a roofless church. He lets himself be marked with the cross, wears the hammer as well, and says the two do not seem to quarrel. The Danes go on calling the place the priests' farm.
endings.reward: Flag en_hostage_given (leave to trade across the line between the armies); Ketil and his heirs friends of the house; a booth plot at the hythe at half price (streonaeshalch.work.booth); the deed carried_letters.

endings.how: You sided with the neighbours and carried dressed stone and lead from the ruins round to the river for pay.
endings.text: A hall by the harbour gets good footings. The priest moves to the last cell with a roof and stops coming down for bread. Ketil's wife does not speak to you.
endings.reward: About 150 d in hack silver and the settlers' easy goodwill; the deed dug_church_ground with every churchman who hears of it.

endings.how: You traded with Ketil, gave the priest alms, and took no side.
endings.text: Nothing changes quickly. The priest dies one winter; another comes, or does not. The name sticks either way.
endings.reward: Ordinary trade at the hythe and the deed gave_alms; no surety, so no leave across the line from here.

stories.reward: A sworn standing among the settlers that the house can use all along the coast of the divided kingdom, or silver and a bad name with the church.

works.name: An iron-bound chest and a cart to Hackness
works.what: A chest of oak with iron straps and a lock from a smith at York, big enough for the house's best books wrapped in waxed cloth, and an ox cart with two laymen to take it over the moor track to the sisters at Hackness, a day's walk from the sea.
works.needs: The abbess's decision, in the story 'Whether the saints should go inland'; iron from York or its price.
works.gives: The house's best books survive the house (the ending chest_to_hackness); the flag bk_carried; Sigethryth copies any text here for nothing; the heir is welcome at Hackness.
works.picture: Two men heaving an iron-strapped chest onto an ox cart outside a low stone building on a windy headland, a small nun checking the knots, moorland beyond.
works.source: Hackness, Hild's daughter house, was standing and in use in these years: its cross carries a prayer for Aethelburh (en.wikipedia Hackness). That books were sent there is the game's; the spine has the house wondering whether to move them.

works.name: Skins for a second Life of Gregory
works.what: The calfskin, ink and red for one fair copy of the Life of Pope Gregory that was written in this house, and the scribe's winter to make it: some twenty skins and a hundred short days.
works.needs: Sigethryth willing (she is, for skins); a winter between two visits.
works.gives: A book in the hold that is the merchant's to carry (bk_carried when it is delivered; the ending copy_over_sea); the scribe teaches what a book is worth (bk_knows_worth).
works.picture: A nun at a sloped desk by a north window in winter light, a stack of pale folded skins beside her and one finished leaf with a red initial drying on a line.
works.source: The Life was written here about 713 (en.wikipedia Gregory the Great). It survives in a single manuscript kept at Saint Gall (memory; Colgrave 1968 not opened) (?): how it got there is unknown, and a merchant's part in it is the game's.

works.name: A stone with a name
works.what: A small slab or a plain cross of the local sandstone, cut with a cross and the name of one of the house's dead, set in the graveyard south of the church among the others.
works.needs: A dead crewman, kinsman or partner to name; the abbess's leave; the scribe to draw the letters.
works.gives: The dead of the house are remembered here (act:remember lifts the crew's heart more than a grave alone); English men who read it think well of the house; the stone is still there for the heirs, and after 867 it is one of the few things here with a name on it.
works.picture: A knee-high plain stone cross with one short name cut across its arms, new and pale among older grey ones, on a cliff-top graveyard with the sea behind.
works.source: Plain crosses and name stones from the abbey: the Corpus of Anglo-Saxon Stone Sculpture lists 56 pieces (the kinds from memory). An instance of works_793.json grave_stone (unlocks_793.json: 120 d, 20 days, Northumbrian ports before 900).

works.name: A booth and a boat-stance at Hvitabyr
works.what: A plot on the river bank measured out by the rope before witnesses: room to draw up one boat, a turf-and-timber booth with a door that bars, and a rack for fish or goods.
works.needs: The holder of the river mouth willing (Ketil, his heirs, or from 1033 the earl's reeve) and two settlers to witness, as their custom asks.
works.gives: Goods can be stored here over a winter (act:store without rent); a factor can be left; the harbour men treat the house as a neighbour, and the plot passes to the heir.
works.picture: A small turf-walled booth with a plank door on a river bank, a boat drawn up beside it bow to the land, two men in settlers' dress pacing out the ground with a knotted rope.
works.source: A substantial town by the harbour by 1066 (English Heritage). Sale before witnesses and the settlers' custom in marks and ores: Design/content/realms/northumbria_york.json. The plot itself is the game's.

works.name: A bell for the priests' farm
works.what: A hand bell of iron dipped in bronze, of the kind a priest rings at the door of his church, brought from York for the one roofed cell on the headland.
works.needs: A priest living at Prestebi; the bell bought at York, or its price sent there.
works.gives: The hours are rung on the headland again and heard at the booths; churchmen along the coast hear of it (standing with the church up); it counts toward the ending bell_hung.
works.picture: A thin priest in a patched cloak ringing a small square hand bell in the doorway of a thatched stone cell, roofless walls all round him and gulls lifting off them.
works.source: The bell that called the sisters at Hackness on the night Hild died: Bede IV.23. Hand bells of sheet iron brazed with bronze are the common early kind (memory) (?). Prestebi: Victoria County History.

ships.note: A tarred fishing boat off the sand under the cliff, sold when a man gets too old for the river bar. Good for the scars, the Esk and a calm day along the coast; not for the open sea.
ships.picture: A small tarred clinker boat lying on her side on wet sand under a high cliff, a net over her gunwale and a sounding pole stuck upright beside her.
ships.source: Boats lay on the drying sand inside the mouth (dossier section 1, inference). Nothing records a boat sale here.

ships.note: The house's own boat, which fetches wine and wax from the Tyne and the Humber and takes cloth to York. Lent, not sold, to a merchant who has kept three commissions for the house and is well regarded here: two thirds of the freight on the house's goods stays the house's.
ships.picture: A broad open boat of ten paces with a single undyed square sail, beached below a headland with roofs on it, a monk and two laymen passing bolts of cloth over her side.
ships.source: story/ships_793.json and unlocks_793.json: the minster ship is lent at streonaeshalch until about 870; traffic_793.json gives the port one such ship. That this house had one is by likeness to other minsters (?).

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: A four- or six-oared boat in the settlers' manner, light and quick to beach, built in a shed by the river from oak cut up the Esk. Ketil's neighbours build them for themselves and will build one more for silver by weight.
ships.picture: A slender new clinker boat on trestles in an open-sided shed by a brown river, pale curled shavings underneath, a man in a settler's tunic driving a rivet.
ships.source: The Danish settlement after 876 (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle) and the town by the harbour before 1066 (English Heritage); oak woods on the Esk. No boat or yard has been dug here (?).

sayings.text: It has much and excellent jet, which is black and sparkling, glittering at the fire, and when heated, drives away serpents; being warmed with rubbing, it holds fast whatever is applied to it, like amber.
sayings.source: Bede, Ecclesiastical History I.1, of Britain (the wording as on sourcebooks.fordham.edu/basis/bede-book1.asp; taken to be Giles 1847 (?))

sayings.text: Nu scylun hergan hefaenricaes uard: now we must honour heaven's guardian.
sayings.source: Caedmon's Hymn, the Northumbrian first line as in the oldest copies (en.wikipedia Caedmon); the English is our own rendering

sayings.text: The king said he would not go against the doorkeeper, in case he came to the gate of heaven and found the one with the keys had turned his back.
sayings.source: Oswiu at the Easter debate here in 664; after Bede III.25, in our own words

sayings.text: Healfden divided the land of the Northumbrians; so that they became afterwards their harrowers and plowers.
sayings.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 876 (avalon.law.yale.edu/medieval/ang09.asp, no translator credited; taken to be Ingram 1823 (?))

sayings.text: There the wood is loud, the ocean-guests' noise; still remain the rocky cliffs from the watery strife.
sayings.source: Exeter Book, the storm riddle, part 3 (texts_793.json exeter_03_storm_sky: Thorpe, Codex Exoniensis, 1842)

sayings.text: Often there is treasure in a sooty bag.
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs, own rendering from the Old English (Design/content/lore/proverbs_jokes.json pj043): said here of the jet gatherers' sacks

sayings.text: He longs the less who knows many songs, or can touch the harp with his hands.
sayings.source: Maxims I (?), own rendering from the Old English (proverbs_jokes.json pj054): said in the guest house, usually at the cowherd

sayings.text: Jet is known by the fire and a neighbour by the hard winter.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, on Bede's test of jet

sayings.text: When the harp comes round, a wise man remembers his cattle.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, on Bede IV.24

sayings.text: My God, almighty God, help Cy...
sayings.source: Runes cut on a bone comb found on the headland, 7th century; the owner's name breaks off (en.wikipedia Anglo-Saxon runes). Said in the house as the prayer of anyone interrupted

easter_eggs.text: A bone comb in the guest house has a prayer cut along its back in runes: 'my God, almighty God, help Cy'. The rest of the owner's name is on the piece that broke off. Nobody remembers who Cy was.
easter_eggs.source: The Whitby comb, 7th century (en.wikipedia Anglo-Saxon runes)

easter_eggs.text: The king on Hunwine's game board is black: a piece of jet turned smooth. Its like will be found in the ground here twelve hundred years on.
easter_eggs.source: A jet gaming piece of the Anglian period (English Heritage, Whitby Abbey research page)

easter_eggs.text: A jet spindle whorl by a loom on the cliff edge has three runes on it: u, e, u. Its owner says it is her mark. It is not a word in any tongue aboard.
easter_eggs.source: The Whitby jet spindle whorl with the runes 'ueu' (en.wikipedia Anglo-Saxon runes)

easter_eggs.text: The coiled stones in the Scar look like snakes without heads. In 793 nobody at the house has a story about them. The story that Abbess Hild turned the snakes to stone comes later, and nobody knows when.
easter_eggs.source: The ammonites of the Whitby shore and the snakestone legend, of unknown date (en.wikipedia Whitby; dossier section 7)

easter_eggs.text: King Edwin lies under his slab without his head. The head is at York, in the church he began there. The body was found at Hatfield, where he fell, by a priest who was shown the place in a dream; this house wrote the story down.
easter_eggs.source: Victoria County History, York North Riding vol. 2; en.wikipedia Edwin of Northumbria; the dream is in the Whitby Life of Gregory (memory) (?)

easter_eggs.text: Among the oddments in the writing-house chest is a lead seal with the name of a Roman archdeacon, Boniface, off a letter nobody has kept.
easter_eggs.source: A lead seal of a papal archdeacon Boniface from the 1920s dig (memory, not opened) (?)

easter_eggs.text: The Life of Pope Gregory written at this desk will survive in one copy only, in a monastery among mountains a long way south. The book that tells of the Angles and the angels outlives every other book the house ever owned.
easter_eggs.source: The single manuscript of the Whitby Life at Saint Gall (memory; Colgrave 1968 not opened) (?)

easter_eggs.text: Sea birds crossing the headland seem to dip as they pass the church. Later people will say they bow their wings to the abbess. In 793 it is put down to the wind off the cliff.
easter_eggs.source: The tradition that sea birds dip their wings to Hild, of unknown date (en.wikipedia Hilda of Whitby)

easter_eggs.text: After 876 the place has two new names at once: Hvitabyr, the white farmstead, down by the boats, and Prestebi, the priests' farm, up among the ruins. Only one of them lasts.
easter_eggs.source: en.wikipedia Whitby; Victoria County History, York North Riding vol. 2 (Prestebi, an 11th-century form)

easter_eggs.text: The brown river holds mussels that now and then have a small dull pearl in them. The fishermen's children know which pools.
easter_eggs.source: The Esk is the only Yorkshire river with freshwater pearl mussels (en.wikipedia River Esk, North Yorkshire; a modern fact carried back) (?)

unlocks.what: The third storm leaf: the storm in the sky
unlocks.how: Be shown the sea chest on the sand under the East Cliff, any year from 799 to 867, in the story 'What the sea gave Cudda'.
unlocks.gives: give_text exeter_03_storm_sky; give_riddle riddle_exeter_03_storm_sky; with the leaves of Lindisfarena and Gyrwe, the landing among the Farne islands (rw_cove_farne).

unlocks.what: A place by name on the guest-house bench
unlocks.how: Bring the abbess true news from the north twice, or end 'When the harp comes round' by singing or by going to the byre.
unlocks.gives: Free lodging (lodge) and broth here until 867; Hunwine's news before the fire's (ask_news); a wounded crewman tended without charge (heal); passes to the heir at half strength, as feeling does.

unlocks.how: Buy fairly at the Scar for three seasons and sell only tested stone (the ending first_pick of 'Black and bright').
unlocks.gives: buy_at_source for jet at the gatherers' price, before the cellar or the booths see it, each spring between Easter and midsummer; holds under the abbey, the settlers and the earl alike.

unlocks.how: Ask a cliff man at the Scar, in any year.
unlocks.gives: flag st_knows_jet: false jet can be told from true in any market (sample never fails on jet), and the cheat can be named before witnesses.

unlocks.what: The house's ship for a season
unlocks.how: As unlocks_793.json has it: keep three commissions for the house and be well regarded here, before 867.
unlocks.gives: Ship class coaster_minster_ship, lent, not owned; two thirds of the freight on the house's goods is the house's; she goes back if she carries captives or arms.

unlocks.what: A name in the house's book of the living and the dead
unlocks.how: A gift of 240 d or its worth, for a dead man of the house, the crew or the partnership (act:remember at the church), with standing of known or better.
unlocks.gives: The name is prayed for while the house stands; standing here does not decay; an heir is known by his father's name. After 867 the book is gone with the house, and only a stone in the graveyard still says it.

unlocks.what: Surety among the settlers of the river mouth
unlocks.how: End 'The priests' farm' with the bell hung, between 883 and 914.
unlocks.gives: flag en_hostage_given; Ketil's kin speak for the house at any settlers' meeting on this coast; the booth plot at half price.

unlocks.what: Caedmon's song, learned in the byre
unlocks.how: Sit with Hwaetred in the byre before 806, or pay Sigethryth for a written leaf before 835.
unlocks.gives: A song the crew can say at any English guest fire (act:song); Beornwine's heart up; at Eoforwic's minster table the merchant is not quite a stranger.
